sentences.text: The genus Wahasuchus is known primarily from fragmentary remains that represent multiple individuals.

The skull's generally flattened morphology, similar to modern crocodiles, suggests it belonged to the Neosuchia clade. Reassembly of available parts suggests the skull was platyrostral, or flattened like that of modern crocodiles. The snout was massively built with expanded individual elements that gave the rostrum significant depth.

There were five alveoli, or tooth sockets, in each premaxilla bone. The maxilla contained 14 teeth. The first wave of tooth enlargement involved the first five teeth, peaking in size at the third maxillary tooth. The second wave of tooth enlargement spanned from the sixth to the fourteenth tooth. The last seven maxillary teeth were confluent, with little to no space between their sockets.

The anterior process of the jugal bone was especially large, being three times as broad as the posterior process. The ventral surface of the jugal bore foramina and pits, while the surface below the eyesockets was marked by shallow grooves. The postorbital bone of Wahasuchus has a triradiate structure with three main sections.

The dentary of Wahasuchus contained at least 16 teeth, with preservation suggesting a total of 17 or 18 teeth. The fourth tooth in the lower jaw of Wahasuchus is the largest and fits into a notch between the upper premaxillary and maxillary teeth.

The genus Wahasuchus was first described in 2018 by Sara Saber and colleagues.

The fossils were discovered in 2010 by researchers from Mansoura University. All known material was collected from an outcrop near Mut in the Dakhla Oasis of Egypt's Western Desert. The fossils are currently held in the collection of the Mansoura University Vertebrate Paleontology Center.
Fossils of Wahasuchus have been found in the Quseir Formation in Egypt. Besides the holotype skull remains, additional fossils from a nearby bonebed were assigned to the genus.
Wahasuchus likely spent much of its time in water and had an opportunistic diet that included turtles, fish, and land vertebrates.
The platyrostral snout shape of Wahasuchus was likely acquired convergently, similar to many other neosuchians and modern crocodilians.

Wahasuchus is classified as an extinct mesoeucrocodylian and is likely a member of the Neosuchia clade. The genus Wahasuchus currently contains only one species, Wahasuchus egyptensis. Features like a flattened skull, enclosed otic opening, and simple dentition suggest Wahasuchus belongs to the group Neosuchia. The amphicoelous nature of Wahasuchus vertebrae suggests it may be an early-diverging member of Neosuchia. The type species of the genus Wahasuchus is Wahasuchus egyptensis.
Wahasuchus lived during the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous. Wahasuchus lived during the Campanian stage, between 83.6 and 72.2 million years ago.

Researchers hypothesize that the quadrate bones had no contact with the exoccipital bone, though they note this might be due to preservation issues. The exact relationship of Wahasuchus with other crocodyliforms remains elusive due to poor fossil preservation, particularly of the palate.
